opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is scale and cost. With human feedback, every preference label requires someone to read two responses, think about them carefully, and decide which is better. That's slow and expensive, so you only get labels on a relatively narrow slice of prompts, usually the common ones you've collected from users or that annotators can handle comfortably.

With AI feedback, once you have a reasonably capable model acting as the judge, generating a label is essentially just another inference call. So you can produce feedback on millions of prompts, including long-tail ones that would rarely show up in a human-labeled dataset: obscure technical questions, unusual formats, multilingual inputs, edge cases in reasoning, and so on. You can even have models generate new prompts specifically to probe areas where the policy is weak, and then critique the responses, which is very hard to do systematically with people.

There's also an expertise angle. Many prompts require specialized knowledge, like advanced math, niche programming languages, or domain-specific science, and finding human annotators who can reliably judge those is difficult. A strong model, especially one guided by explicit principles or able to check its work, can give at least reasonable signal across a much broader spread of domains.

That said, it's not a free lunch. AI feedback inherits the biases and blind spots of the judging model, and if you're not careful you can end up optimizing toward whatever that judge happens to like rather than what's actually good. So I see it less as a replacement for human feedback and more as a way to amplify it: humans set the principles and audit the hard cases, and AI feedback extends that signal across a far wider range of prompts than people could ever cover directly.

r001.rationale: The response says AI feedback can cover millions of long-tail prompts, but does not state that it could cover arbitrary prompts when models can autonomously generate answers.

r002.rationale: The response mentions difficulty finding experts for specialized topics, but not research needed to verify claims about little-known people as a bottleneck to scaling human feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason comes down to cost and scale. When you rely on human feedback, every label is expensive. You have to recruit annotators, train them, pay them, and wait for them. That naturally pushes you toward a fairly narrow slice of prompts, usually the ones that are easy to write guidelines for and easy for a typical annotator to judge quickly. So you end up with a lot of data on things like general chat, summarization, maybe some coding, and very little on the long tail.

With AI feedback, the marginal cost of a judgment is close to zero. That changes what you can afford to cover. You can generate prompts across thousands of domains, including ones that would be hard to staff with humans, like specialized scientific questions, niche programming languages, or very long multi-step tasks where a person would get tired or inconsistent halfway through. The model doesn't get bored, and it can apply the same rubric millions of times.

There's also a consistency argument. Human raters disagree with each other a lot, and that noise limits how finely you can distinguish between responses. A model judge, if it's calibrated well, can give you a more uniform signal, which lets you learn from subtler differences and from prompts where the right answer isn't obvious to a non-expert.

Now, I want to be careful here. The judge model inherits its own blind spots, so if it's wrong about some domain, you can end up reinforcing that error at scale. So I don't see AI feedback as a replacement for human judgment. I think of it more as a way to amplify a smaller amount of high-quality human input. You use humans to define what good looks like and to audit the hard cases, and then you use the model to extend that signal across a much wider distribution of prompts than any human labeling effort could realistically reach.

r002.rationale: The response discusses human-labeling cost and annotator limits, but does not identify research to verify claims about little-known people as a scaling bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is scale. With human feedback, you need someone to look at the model’s responses and judge which one is better. That takes time, so you’re limited in how many prompts you can cover and how many responses you can evaluate for each prompt. With AI feedback, you can do that across a much larger and more diverse set of prompts, including situations that might be rare in a human-labeled dataset.

Of course, that doesn’t mean the feedback is always correct. You’re still limited by what the AI evaluator can reliably judge. But if you can get a useful feedback signal, you can apply it much more broadly, while using human feedback to help check and guide that process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main advantage is scale. With human feedback, you need someone to look at the model’s responses and judge which one is better, and there’s a limit to how many people you can hire and how many different prompts they can evaluate. With AI feedback, you can apply that process to a much larger and more diverse set of prompts, including ones that might come up relatively rarely.

Of course, that doesn’t mean the feedback is always correct. You’re still limited by what the AI evaluator can reliably judge, and you can reinforce its biases or mistakes. But if you have a reasonably good evaluator, you can get much broader coverage, while using human feedback to help check and calibrate those judgments.
